About 100 people participate in a lottery to divide a 12 acre plot of sand dunes that would later become the city of Tel Aviv, 1909

On 11 April 1909, 66 Jewish families gathered on a desolate sand dune to parcel out the land by lottery using seashells. This gathering is considered the official date of the establishment of Tel Aviv. The lottery was organised by Akiva Aryeh Weiss, president of the building society. Weiss collected 120 sea shells on the beach, half of them white and half of them grey. The members' names were written on the white shells and the plot numbers on the grey shells. A boy drew names from one box of shells and a girl drew plot numbers from the second box. A photographer, Avraham Soskin, documented the event.

And how important is skill level in creating an enjoyable co-op experience?
Is it better to have one co-op buddy that's highly skilled, or both co-op buddies be moderately skilled?

For me it matter more to match the skill level of the game itself. Co-op games have a "minimum required skill" effect, where one person having trouble often means both players having trouble (and nobody having fun). On the other hand, one player being exceptionally skilled at a game can be a problem if the player just blows through the objectives of the game single-handedly. Ideally both players would meet the minimum skill level for the game without being too uneven, but when one player is more experienced than the other, being courteous of your co-op buddy makes a world of difference.

It can also depend on the game, in some cases having one more skilled is not a huge issue as they can take a more difficult role, fore example as a scout that is quick and light to move but has less armor/weapons. This give the team an advantage of knowing what is going on but in a fight that player is handy-capped while the other has more gear substituting for skill.

For me and my main co-op buddy we have slightly different preferences and this can determine who is the better or more informed about a game. There can also be differences in the players that can lead to the role they play for example I tend to be quick to memorize levels so often lead through area that are replayed until he gets them down as well, I have an extreme annoyance with bad random level systems at one point when playing it regularly I could guide through the "random" level in Diablo 3 with about 85% accuracy due to recognizing patterns. However he is much better about finding info about a game from others in videos where I like to either skim some text or trial by fire. He is also better at focusing on a task until completion in things like Minecraft where I will wander off to try something else if it takes excessive time dedication and I get bored.

If you work with one person long enough you know what they do best and you can choose roles to fit your skills. Though sometimes this backfires. Diablo 2 we played like addicts back in the early 2000s he favored his barbarian I my Necromancer (pure bone build) He tanked I applied DPS, come Diablo 3 we tried this layout and neither had fun nor did we progress. Came back to D3 later and things went well with his Witch Doctor and my Crusader he killed fast and I just wouldn't die. Sometimes I would get things I would stalemate with and could not kill this was resolved when he got done with his group and applied more dps to mine but without me the whole would have been to much for him to kill before being taken down.
Man, that's a better answer than I could have hoped for. I hadn't thought about how different aptitudes can influence roles in-game.
